title: Sin embargo and no obstante: contrasting two ideas

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know contrast connectors like *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1. They begin the second sentence and say that it goes against what you might expect after the first: *Al principio el encuentro fue pacífico. Sin embargo, pronto empezaron los conflictos.*

items.spanish: Al principio el encuentro fue pacífico. Sin embargo, pronto empezaron los conflictos.
items.english: At first the encounter was peaceful. However, conflicts soon began.

items.spanish: Los dos pueblos hablaban lenguas distintas. No obstante, hubo intercambio de palabras.
items.english: The two peoples spoke different languages. Nevertheless, words were exchanged.

items.spanish: Había poco oro en las islas. Sin embargo, los españoles exigían cada vez más.
items.english: There was little gold on the islands. However, the Spanish demanded more and more.

items.spanish: Los taínos recibieron a los españoles con amistad; no obstante, los españoles buscaban oro.
items.english: The Taíno received the Spanish with friendship; nevertheless, the Spanish were looking for gold.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* mean the same; *no obstante* sounds a little more formal. Put a comma after them. In a long sentence they can follow a semicolon, as in the last example. Do not use *por eso* here: that connector shows a result, not a contrast.
